trail.title: How sound happens
trail.intro: Sound is pushes in the air. To keep a song, a machine must turn the pushes into numbers it can hold, and to play it, back again. This is the trail of that trick, from ear to number.

step.name: pressure
step.line: a wave of pushes in the air
step.blurb: Sound is pressure. A drum, a voice, a speaker cone pushes the air, the push travels as a wave, and your eardrum is shoved in time with it. A single note is the air swinging back and forth a few hundred times a second; nothing solid ever moves from the singer to you, only the push.

door.q: Is a picture caught the same way?
How does a push in the air become a number at all?

step.name: the diaphragm
step.line: a little drum that turns push into voltage
step.blurb: A microphone holds a tiny drum, thinner than a hair. Each arriving push bends it, the bending drags a magnet through a coil of wire, and the wire answers with a wobbling voltage: the push, copied as electricity. The wave is still continuous, still in time with the song.

door.q: Another sheet that turns a push into numbers?
Measured, rounded, numbered — the picture too?
The ear has its drum; the eye has its wells — light caught the same way

step.name: sampling
step.line: measured 44,100 times every second
step.blurb: A machine cannot hold a continuous wobble, so it measures it: 44,100 quick snapshots every second, each one the voltage at that instant. The number is not arbitrary. The ear tops out near twenty thousand waves a second, and measuring at least twice per wave rebuilds every wave the ear can hear; the compact disc chose 44,100, and the number stayed.

door.q: Who gives the beat?
Measured 44,100 times every second — who counts a second?

step.name: rounding
step.line: each measurement, one of 65,536 steps
step.blurb: Each snapshot is rounded to the nearest of 65,536 steps and written down as a number. The rounding is honest, the true voltage almost never exactly on a step, but the steps are so fine that the rebuilt wave is indistinguishable, to an ear, from the original. One rounded number is called a sample.

door.q: Pictures are caught the same way: measured, rounded, numbered.
65,536 steps — how is a step spelled?

step.name: the file
step.line: a small note, then millions of numbers
step.blurb: A WAV file is a small header (44,100 a second, 16 bits per sample, two ears) followed by millions of samples in order, one per ear per moment. The file is a long column of numbers and a note about how to read it, and nothing else.

door.q: Where do millions of numbers wait?
Who keeps the files?

step.name: the bytes
step.line: each number spelled in sixteen binary digits
step.blurb: A sample can hold any of 65,536 values, and 65,536 is 2¹⁶, so each sample is spelled in sixteen binary digits, split into two bytes of eight. A three-minute song is some thirty million bytes: an entire performance pressed into a column of numbers, in the alphabet the whole machine speaks.

door.q: Where do the two symbols come from?
Where do the numbers park?

trail.bottom: Push to voltage, voltage to number, number to digits: this is how the machine keeps anything at all.

door.q: The Bit — the alphabet of two symbols
Memory — where a song waits while it plays

trail.title: How an image happens
trail.intro: A picture is a wall of lamps obeying numbers. To draw, the machine must turn light into numbers, numbers into memory, and memory back into light, in time. This is the trail, from lamp to number and back.

step.name: one lamp
step.line: told how much red, green and blue to be
step.blurb: One pixel is three lamps pressed close together: red, green, blue. Each is told, by a number, how brightly to shine, and the three mix in the eye — full of all three is white, none of them is black. That is the whole of colour on every screen you own.

door.q: Is sound caught the same way?
How does brightness become a number at all?

step.name: three numbers
step.line: a pixel is a trio, each 0 to 255
step.blurb: Each lamp’s brightness is rounded to one of 256 steps, 0 to 255 — one byte each, the same rounding the ear forgave. A pixel is therefore three numbers, and numbers can be written down, copied and sent like any others. To the machine a photograph is not a picture; it is an enormous list.

door.q: Sound too is numbers — measured, rounded
The list is enormous — but how is the light caught to begin with?

step.name: the grid
step.line: two million trios, one picture
step.blurb: A television frame is 1,920 columns by 1,080 rows of these trios — about two million pixels, six million numbers. There is no image in the machine anywhere, only the list; the screen is where the list is interpreted. Every photograph ever shown on a computer has been this.

door.q: Where do two million trios live?
How does a screen’s worth cross the wire?

step.name: the frame in memory
step.line: the picture lives in a block of memory
step.blurb: The six million numbers of one frame sit together in one region of memory, the frame buffer, and the screen rereads it wholesale, dozens of times a second. The picture is not in the screen; it is a block of ordinary memory, and the screen is its window.

door.q: How a circuit holds six million numbers against time.
Who owns the block of numbers?

step.name: drawing is writing
step.line: to move something, change numbers
step.blurb: Every stroke of every game and every film is arithmetic on the buffer: move a character ten pixels right and the machine adds ten across a few hundred thousand numbers, fills in behind, shades the edge. The programmers never touch a lamp. They arrange for numbers to change — and deciding which numbers change is a different, older question.

door.q: Who decides, and how? The trail of choices.
What if two programs draw at once?
Who does this arithmetic by the million? The trail of the thousand painters
The painters live on one chip — how a game chip learned math

step.name: the beat
step.line: whatever is in the buffer is what you see
step.blurb: A clock beats, and on each beat the screen repaints from the buffer, top to bottom, while the machine races to finish its changes before the next one. A moving image is a list rewritten in time with a clock; miss the beat and the picture tears, win it and everything moves.

door.q: The switching illusion — who repaints your world?
What holds the frame between beats?

trail.bottom: Light rounded to numbers, numbers held in memory, memory repainted in time. At the bottom, each of these numbers is spelled in the machine’s alphabet.

door.q: The Bit — the spelling of every number
The trail of the machine — what does the painting

trail.title: How anything becomes a number
trail.intro: The machine’s world is a column of numbers, but the world itself is not numbers: it is pressure, brightness, heat, position, arriving continuously and never sitting still. This is the trail of the crossing, the same few moves every sensor makes, from the world to one written number.

step.name: the senses
step.line: the world arrives as a wobble of voltage
step.blurb: Nothing in the world arrives as a number. A sound is a shove in the air. Light is a rain of small packets. Heat is a jostling. Each has a go-between built for it (a diaphragm, a tiny well, a strip of metal that resists more as it warms), and every go-between answers the same way: with a voltage that rises and falls as the world does. The voltage is still the world, still continuous, still refusing to hold still. Numbers have not entered yet.

door.q: The diaphragm — sound’s own go-between
Brightness caught as voltage — the same trick
A lattice of tiny wells, one for each point of light

step.name: the hold
step.line: one instant, frozen while it is read
step.blurb: A voltage that never stops moving cannot be read, so the machine cheats fairly: for an instant it opens a switch and lets a small cup of charge hold the voltage still, the value at this exact moment frozen, then reads the frozen copy at leisure, and opens the switch again for the next moment. Thousands of times a second, sometimes millions, the world is caught, held, and let go. The frozen instant is the only thing the machine ever measures; the rest of the world flows past unread.

door.q: Who says when to freeze — the beat, counted
A charge held still while it is read — how does a machine remember at all?

step.name: the ruler
step.line: a ladder of known values, and one question
step.blurb: To read a frozen voltage, the machine compares it against values it knows how to make. It builds a ladder of rungs, each rung a number turned back into a voltage, and climbs by asking one question, over and over: is the world above this rung, or below? The cleverness is in the asking — not counting rung by rung from the bottom, but halving. Twelve honest questions place a value among 4,096 rungs; sixteen place it among 65,536. Finding a number is a game of yes-or-no, and the machine is very good at yes-or-no.

door.q: Every halving is a fork — the yes-or-no game in full
The ladder, walked the other way: numbers become voltages

step.name: the staircase
step.line: the true value, landed on the nearest rung
step.blurb: The world’s value is almost never exactly on a rung, so it is landed on the nearest one and written down as that rung’s number. This is rounding, and it is honest: the gap between rungs is a small standing error, paid on every measurement. But the staircase can be made as fine as anyone can afford: the compact disc’s staircase has 65,536 steps, and no ear has ever found one. Every number the machine holds about the world stands on some staircase like this, one rung chosen from a ladder.

door.q: 65,536 steps — the song’s own staircase
The rounded row becomes a world — what simulations eat

step.name: the row
step.line: one number written down, then another, then another
step.blurb: One measurement is one number; the world is the row that follows. Sample by sample the numbers are written in order, 44,100 of them for each second of song, a whole lattice of them for each frame of film, and the row is the world as the machine will ever know it: parked in memory, poured down a wire, argued over by programs. Nothing upstream checks whether the row is true. Whatever the rungs said, the row now is.

door.q: Where the row parks, and how it is found again
The row poured out — a stream is a message too

trail.bottom: Sense, freeze, halve, land, write: five moves, and the world is a column of numbers. Every trail in this deck begins where this one ends.

door.q: The Bit — the alphabet every rung is spelled in
The gate — the small etched judge that answers above or below

trail.title: How a message travels
trail.intro: No wire runs from your phone to the restaurant. Your order crosses in small numbered pieces, handed from machine to machine, and is rebuilt at the far end. This is the trail of a message.

step.name: chopping
step.line: a long message becomes small packets
step.blurb: A wire can carry only so much at once, and a long message would jam every machine along its road. So the sender chops it: the order becomes a handful of small packets (at most 1,500 bytes on the wires that carry most of the internet) sent separately across a road many strangers share. Small is also survival arithmetic: a wire flips a bit perhaps once in ten thousand, and a 1,000-bit packet therefore crosses intact about nine times in ten, while a 20,000-bit packet survives barely one trip in seven and must be sent again and again. The packet is sized so that most packets do not meet an error at all. Nothing crosses whole; everything crosses in pieces, cut to the rate of the road and the noise on it.

door.q: Numbers all the way down — what carries them?
A long story chopped into small words — how small can a language get?

step.name: the envelope
step.line: every packet labelled with numbers
step.blurb: Each piece is wrapped in an envelope (where from, where to, which piece of the whole this is), and every machine on the network has a number of its own, four bytes such as 142.250.72.14. The envelope also carries a proof of itself: a few extra bits, folded from the packet’s own numbers, that let the far end check the packet arrived unscrambled and throw it away otherwise. A packet spoiled by a cosmic ray or a neighbour’s noisy motor is discarded exactly like a packet that never came. The envelope is written in the same numbers as the message. No router can read your order; every router can read the envelope.

door.q: What is inside the machines doing the handing?
An address finds one machine among millions — how are places found again?
No router can read the order — how is a message made unreadable?

step.name: hop to hop
step.line: no road goes all the way
step.blurb: At each crossroads a router reads the address and hands the packet down the best next wire; no router holds the whole road, and each is responsible only for the next hop. The tables are built by many machines, none seeing the whole, and they can disagree, a disagreement that can send a packet in a circle until it eats the very road it rides. So every envelope carries a countdown: one byte, set to about sixty-four by the sender, ticked down by every router, the packet dropped at zero: the looping packet must die so the rest keep moving. The route can change mid-message, and the pieces of one order may travel different roads. The internet is not a web of wires to places. It is a crowd of small machines, each deciding the next hop, cooperating without a king, at the price of a countdown in every envelope.

door.q: What stands at each hop?
Many packets, one wire — who goes first?
Some hops hang in the sky — the machines that carry them

step.name: reassembly
step.line: the pieces arrive out of order and are rebuilt
step.blurb: The pieces may arrive out of order: they may travel different roads, and each hop reads a packet whole before it sends it on, so every machine on the road adds its own reading delay. But each envelope says which piece it is, so the receiver rebuilds the whole before anyone reads it. The building is pure bookkeeping: nothing is decoded along the way, only numbered, held briefly, and re-sequenced at the far end. The number on the envelope is what makes confetti a message. Lose the numbering and no wire, however fast, can deliver an order.

door.q: Where do the pieces wait?
Who does the rebuilding?

step.name: keep until received
step.line: a copy held until the far end answers
step.blurb: A packet can vanish in a crowd, dropped at a crossroads or spoiled by noise, so the sender numbers each piece, keeps a copy, and starts a clock: if the far end has not said received when the clock runs out, the piece is sent again. The rule is old and has a name, retransmit on timeout, and its naive version, one piece in flight at a time, is safe but slow, so the sender keeps a whole window of numbered pieces in the air at once, and each answer that comes back slides the window forward. The reliability lives at the two ends, not in the wires. That one small rule lets ten thousand strangers share one planet of wires without losing their words. And it is the same rule that keeps two riders off one order.

door.q: Two hands, one order book: the oldest bug, and the cure.
A copy held — held where?
A copy held until the far end answers — the rule money runs on

trail.bottom: Chopped, numbered, handed onward, rebuilt: everything you have ever sent travelled as numbers in envelopes.

door.q: The Bit — envelopes and addresses are numbers
The trail of the machine — what a router is

trail.title: How a secret crosses
trail.intro: The wire was built to survive, not to hide: every envelope is readable by every machine that hands it on. Yet your card number crosses it every day. This is the trail of how — the goals a secret must state, the one key both ends must share, the strangers’ trick that builds a shared secret in the open, the two keys that let anyone lock, and the traitor the whole scheme exists to catch.

step.name: the open wire
step.line: the road was built to survive, not to hide
step.blurb: The internet’s design goal was survival, not secrecy: the wires were made to keep working when parts of the network were destroyed, and nothing in the design hides what they carry. Any stranger on the road can keep a copy of every envelope that passes him. So everything private must state its goals exactly, and there are three: the eavesdropper must not be able to read the message (confidentiality), the receiver must be able to prove it arrived exactly as sent (integrity), and the receiver must be able to verify who sent it (authentication). The wire cannot be made private. The message can — with numbers, travelling the same open road as everything else.

door.q: the message it rides — chopped, numbered, handed onward, rebuilt
the listener is not an accident — the failure this whole trail designs against

step.name: the shared key
step.line: one key does the locking and the opening, and it must arrive somehow
step.blurb: The workhorse of secrecy is the shared key: a number, 128 to 256 bits long, known to the two ends and to no one else, used to scramble what leaves and unscramble what arrives. Fast, orders of magnitude faster than the public arithmetic two steps down, and strong: against a good cipher there is no known shortcut, only the trying of every key, and a 256-bit search is beyond any effort that fits in a universe. But the key itself must arrive somehow, and the wire is public: the courier with the briefcase, the old answer, has no descendant here. This is the chicken-and-egg at the heart of secrecy: how to share a secret over a line on which every listener sits.

door.q: the scrambling is arithmetic — the machine’s own numbers, rearranged
the key, kept — how a machine holds what it must find again and never lose

step.name: the strangers’ mixing
step.line: a shared secret built in the open
step.blurb: Two strangers who have never met can build a shared secret in public. They agree, out loud, on a large prime (several hundred digits) and a small generator. Alice picks a secret exponent and posts the generator raised to it; Bob does the same with his own secret. Each then raises the other’s public number to their own private power, and both arrive at the same value: a shared key, manufactured out loud from pieces the whole world heard. An eavesdropper holding every piece faces the discrete logarithm: recovering the hidden exponent from the public result is believed all but impossible when the prime is large enough. The arithmetic runs one way, easy forward and intractable backwards, like water downhill.

door.q: the staircase walked backwards — the value given, the rung asked for
the meeting in the open — two strangers agreeing without a private room

step.name: the two keys
step.line: a lock anyone can snap shut, one key that opens
step.blurb: The other answer splits the key in two. One half, the public key, is published to the world: anyone may use it to lock a message for its owner, and only the private half, kept by the owner alone, opens what the public one has locked. RSA builds the pair from two large primes: the public key is their product, with locking instructions; the private key needs the factors back, and multiplying is quick while factoring is a search whose cost grows explosively with every added digit. Run the pair backwards and it becomes a signature: a digest sealed with the private key, verifiable by anyone holding the public one: proof that the owner, and no one else, sealed it. The lock is free to all, only one hand can open, and reversed, it is a voice no one can forge.

door.q: one published key, millions of strangers — the lock everyone can use together
the signature — a sealed claim any stranger can verify: the rule money runs on

step.name: the traitor in the middle
step.line: the stranger who answers in Bob’s name
step.blurb: The arithmetic is not the weak point. The meeting is. In the middle of the exchange a traitor can answer in Bob’s name: Alice locks her message with Mallory’s key, believing it is Bob’s. Mallory reads it, and re-locks it with the real Bob’s. The cipher never breaks — the trust does. The cure is vouching, not mathematics: Bob’s key, signed by someone Alice already trusts, dated to expire because trust erodes. At the small scale, keys are signed at parties into a web of trust; at the large scale, certificate authorities the browser already trusts, the strange inherited confidence behind the padlock in the address bar. And the newest handshakes seal each letter with a key thrown away after the reading, so that a key broken tomorrow cannot unseal what was said yesterday.

door.q: the certificate — checked, pinned, expired on time: the watched trust
the trusted parts fail too — revocation and expiry, a trust that must outlive its members

trail.bottom: A public wire, a shared key, a trick of mixing, a lock the world can close, and the vouching that catches the traitor: this is how a secret crosses. Underneath, it is the numbers themselves (every key and every cipher is arithmetic) and the order that keeps an old answer from working twice.

door.q: The Bit — the spelling of every key: secrets are numbers, scrambled by arithmetic
Time — the primer of order: the fresh answer, and the old one that must not count

trail.title: Who runs the machine
trail.intro: Your phone seems to do twenty things at once. It does one at a time, very fast, with a manager. This is the trail of the manager.

step.name: one at a time
step.line: the processor does one thing per instant
step.blurb: However much seems to be happening, the processor executes one instruction at a time, one per beat. Two programs cannot share a moment. Every claim of simultaneity on your phone is an arrangement built on that single fact, and the arrangement has a name.

door.q: What is the one thing?
Who decides what the one thing is?

step.name: the illusion
step.line: switching so fast it looks like everything at once
step.blurb: The trick is switching: a sliver of one program, then a sliver of the next, thousands of times a second, with each one’s whereabouts kept in memory between its turns. None of them notices the gaps. The twenty simultaneous programs are a stage illusion, run very well and very fast.

door.q: The dance, billions of times a second
The switching is a decision

step.name: the scheduler
step.line: a program that decides who goes next
step.blurb: Who goes next is decided by a program, the scheduler — the one program allowed to stop the others and start them again, thousands of times a second. It is a program like any other, running on the same machine by the same rules: a shepherd that is also a sheep, merely trusted.

door.q: How does a machine decide anything at all?
Two programs, one instant — what keeps them apart?

step.name: files
step.line: named blocks of numbers on a disk
step.blurb: A program not running is a file: a named block of bytes on a disk, beside your photographs and your orders. The file is not the program, only its frozen numbers, read back into memory and continued when called. A disk is memory that does not mind waiting.

door.q: How a circuit holds anything at all.
A disk is what, exactly?
A file is a program’s frozen numbers — translated from what?

step.name: the gatekeeper
step.line: one program allowed to touch everything
step.blurb: Memory, disks, the wire, the screen: every program wants them, and only one program is allowed to hand them out — the operating system. Your apps never touch the hardware; they ask, and the manager grants or refuses. That is why one crashing app does not take the phone down with it: the failure stops at the door.

door.q: What may the one program touch?
Who stops two hands on one cell?

trail.bottom: The manager, the scheduler, the files: all of it is programs, and all programs are instructions stored and obeyed. Under the manager stands the machine itself.

door.q: The trail of the machine — what the manager runs
Time — when two hands meet one cell

trail.title: The machine itself
trail.intro: Every trail on this deck ends in a program being obeyed. This is what obeying means: the stored program, from a 1945 sketch to the phone in your hand.

step.name: the radical idea
step.line: store the instructions with the data, in advance
step.blurb: Before 1945 a machine was rewired for each new job; the program was the wiring. The idea that ended that: keep the instructions in the same memory as the data, written down in advance, and let one machine run any job by reading them. The machine no longer changes for the work. The work is a list, and the list is numbers.

door.q: The manager is stored too
Instructions stored like data — how one machine can be any machine
Where the radical idea was first thought — how a thought became a machine

step.name: a number that means a command
step.line: the cell decides by position which it is
step.blurb: In memory a program looks like nothing at all: numbers in cells, indistinguishable from data. The number 108 in one cell is an instruction, load, and the same 108 elsewhere is a piece of data. The difference is not in the cell; it is where the machine is looking. Code is data, and attention makes it code.

door.q: A vocabulary of a few dozen words — the one-word tradition
Load is one of a few dozen words
Programs are written in words — who turns the words into numbers?

step.name: the dance
step.line: fetch, decode, execute — billions of times a second
step.blurb: The machine runs one round forever: fetch the next instruction, decode what its number means (add, load, jump), execute it, move on. Billions of rounds a second, on the beat of a clock. Nothing else is happening inside the phone, the console, the router or the television; every one of them runs this one dance.

door.q: Who shares one machine among many programs?
The dance, step by step

step.name: the one design
step.line: in every box on every trail
step.blurb: The console, the courier’s phone, the warehouse server, the router, the player in the television: one design, scaled and costumed, in every box this deck has walked. Von Neumann’s group sketched it in 1945; the world has built it in the billions since, and nothing has replaced it.

door.q: The whole machine, small enough to step through
Is there anything it cannot do?

trail.bottom: One dance, in every machine you own. The whole machine, small enough to step through by hand, is a primer — and so is the question of what it can never do.

door.q: A real machine — the dance, step by step, for your hands
The Turing machine — what such a machine can never do

trail.title: How a number moves a thing
trail.crumb: how a number moves a thing
trail.intro: Every trail in this deck ends with the machine holding a number. The valve opens, the cone shoves the air, the wheel turns: this is the trail of the last step, where a number stops being arithmetic and starts being a push.

step.name: the number at the edge
step.line: the dance ends holding a number
step.blurb: The dance of fetch, decode and execute ends the same way every time: a number sits in a register, and nothing in the world has moved yet. The number might be a loudness, a position, an opening, a thrust; to the machine it is only bits, waiting. The last mile of every computation is not arithmetic at all. It is matter, and it must be told.

door.q: The dance that ends holding the number
The vocabulary of commands — light, throttle, stop

step.name: the valve
step.line: a voltage that opens and closes a road
step.blurb: The telling is done by the smallest valve there is: a strip of treated sand with a road for current through it and a third wire hung above. Voltage on the third wire and the road opens; voltage off and it closes — a number, arrived as a voltage, steering a current that can be far larger than itself, one switch letting a small signal command a big river. A billion of these valves open and close inside the phone in your pocket, millions of times a second, and the same valve, made fatter, opens a rocket engine’s throttle.

door.q: Open or closed — the one yes-or-no underneath
Where the trick works hardest: a sealed machine in the sky, its thrusters told by number

step.name: the push
step.line: a current through a coil, and the world shoves back
step.blurb: A current moving through a wire sits in a magnetic field, and the field shoves sideways: current becomes force. Coil the wire and the shove becomes a push along the line — a speaker cone shoved in time with the song’s numbers, a motor turned by wishing it so many steps, a valve rammed open against fire. The microphone’s diaphragm is the speaker walked backwards: there a push became a voltage, here a voltage becomes a push. Every output the machine owns ends in this one crossing.

door.q: The speaker — the microphone’s trick, walked backwards
The valve itself — a gate, etched in sand

step.name: the loop
step.line: shove, read, correct, shove again
step.blurb: One shove is never trusted. The machine reads back what its push did, the tilt it caused, the temperature it moved, the speed it changed, compares the reading against the number it wanted, and shoves again, corrected, thousands of times a second. The reading is another trail entirely, the comparison is arithmetic, and the correction is another push. Hold a drone level, a rocket on its lean, an oven at its heat: the same wheel, turning.

door.q: How the world is read back — the other half of the boundary
The plan, computed in advance and walked against the world

step.name: the deadline
step.line: not fast, but on time
step.blurb: When the shove is holding a car in its lane or a rocket on its lean, late is as bad as wrong: the push must arrive on the beat, every beat, or the correction that needed it becomes the accident it feared. This is why most processors are not the computers we think of as computers — they live inside things, and their work has a deadline. The manager in there is a different creature from a laptop’s: it does not share fairly, it guarantees. The valve does not get the processor when convenient. It gets it now.

door.q: The manager who guarantees a beat, not shares one
What a clock is, that a beat can be promised

trail.bottom: Register, valve, coil, loop, deadline: this is how the machine’s numbers leave the machine. The dance above ends in arithmetic; the world below begins in matter.

door.q: The gate — the valve, etched smallest
The dance — the number’s side of the crossing

trail.title: How a machine decides
trail.intro: Jump if the button is pressed and the feet are on the ground. Send again if the answer never came. Grant the next slice to whoever has waited longest. Every decision a program makes is a fork, and the forks themselves are wired.

step.name: one question
step.line: every decision is yes or no
step.blurb: A program decides by asking: is the button pressed? is the count zero? is this address mine? Each question has two answers, and the program takes one road or the other. All the branching richness of software, menus, autopilots, this deck, is a braid of two-answer forks.

door.q: Is the answer found by walking rules? — how it finds the answer
Or guessed from what came before — how a machine improves its guesses

step.name: and, or, not
step.line: the everyday words are the wiring diagram
step.blurb: Jump if pressed AND on the ground. Fire if either button is pressed: OR. Move unless paused: NOT. The words that combine questions in daily speech are the exact ones the machine needs, and each is a small circuit of switches that answers the combined question electrically, in an instant, with nobody home.

door.q: Three words for every decision — how small can a language get?
Programs are made of these words — who checks them?

step.name: the gate
step.line: a question etched in sand
step.blurb: That circuit is called a logic gate: a few pieces of carefully poisoned sand that turn voltages into an answer. AND, OR, NOT, and three or four cousins are the complete vocabulary of decision — the smallest parts of the machine that can be said to know anything.

door.q: The whole vocabulary, for your hands
What are gates good for?

step.name: billions of forks
step.line: the day’s work of a processor
step.blurb: Sixty times a second the game asks a few million of these questions. The scheduler asks who has waited longest. The router asks which wire is best. Every if in every program, unwound far enough, lands on gates — questions etched in sand, answered billions of times a second, honestly, because honestly is all a gate can be.

door.q: Where the forks are taken
How fast is a decision?

trail.bottom: Decision, wired. The whole vocabulary, six gates, one picture, every truth table, is a primer, and it is the piece the rest of the machine is made from.

door.q: Gates — the whole vocabulary, for your hands
The Bit — what the gates are made of

trail.title: How a satellite works
trail.intro: A satellite is a computer in a sealed box, hung where no one can reach it, told what to do by radio, and pouring numbers down without pause. The weather model and the blue dot both begin in that stream. This is the trail of the machine: how it is run, what it senses, and how its numbers arrive.

step.name: the machine aboard
step.line: a computer no one can repair
step.blurb: A satellite is the same machine as the phone in your pocket, sealed in a box nobody will ever open. There is no air to carry the heat away (the sunlit face and the shadow face swing two hundred degrees apart), no hand to press reset, and the sky is full of particles that flip a number in memory now and then. So the machine is built to notice and to be forgiven: it checks its own arithmetic, reports its own voltages and temperatures, restarts itself when a number goes strange, and when a part cannot be forgiven, its work is moved aside, to a reserve aboard or a twin already in orbit, drifted into place. Nothing aboard is ever repaired; everything aboard is built to be forgiven.

door.q: The one design, in every box — even this one
A particle can flip a number — how a circuit holds numbers against the sky

step.name: the senses
step.line: the Earth, read from above into numbers
step.blurb: The machine is up there to sense: cameras for the clouds, infrared for the heat of fields and fires, microwave ears for the wetness of the air. Every instrument does what every instrument in this deck does (measure, round to a number, hand the number on), and the weather model’s first numbers arrive this way, a whole sky every few minutes. The reading half of the forecast starts here, before any arithmetic is walked.

door.q: The eye’s wells, catching the light
Measured, rounded, numbered — the world read like a song

step.name: the commanded word
step.line: ordered by radio, one word at a time
step.blurb: No hand reaches the machine, so everything it does is told to it: a command list uploaded on the radio, checked, and obeyed: spin up, take the picture, hold, sleep. The vocabulary is small, exact, and counted when the machine is built: every command it will ever be allowed to hear is listed years before launch, and the machine never improvises; that is the point. A satellite is not operated so much as it is recited to, and it answers in numbers, its own health poured back on the same small channel, the telling and the telling-what-to-do riding together, one link up, one link down.

door.q: A language small enough for a sky
Every command a yes-or-no fork
The word that fires a thruster — how does a word push?

step.name: the stream home
step.line: the numbers poured down without being asked
step.blurb: The talk home never stops: pictures, readings, and the machine’s own numbers (voltages, temperatures, the state of its wheels) poured down continuously, chopped and wrapped and numbered like any message, kept until the ground says received. It is a few watts of whisper, thinned by tens of thousands of kilometres, and it still arrives, because the wire’s rules do not care how far the wire is. And the same sealed box, hired out as a relay, does even less: a bent pipe, translating the frequency and passing everything on untouched, noise included: one design, two jobs, pouring its own numbers home or faithfully repeating others’. The weather model drinks this stream; so does the blue dot.

door.q: Chopped, numbered, kept until received — the trail of a message
What the stream is spelled in

step.name: the ground beneath
step.line: the control room, the machine’s other half
step.blurb: Half the satellite is on the ground: a room of machines watching the stream, walking the machine’s numbers forward, composing the next command list and reading it up. The rooms sit where the sky is widest, near the equator, the whole arc in view, two antennas so that one is always spare, and the loss of the whole machine is priced before it happens: capacity drawn from reserve, a spare drifted into place, the service interrupted for minutes rather than years. When a number goes strange, the ground decides whether to care; when a burn is needed, the ground prices it. The box in the sky and the room on the ground are one system, and neither half is in charge alone: the manager is the pair of them.

door.q: Who runs a machine you cannot touch?
Where a day of sky parks until the model needs it

step.name: the clock in the sky
step.line: the same stream, carrying here-and-now
step.blurb: The positioning machines stream too, but what they pour is not pictures; it is a sentence (I am here, and my clock says now) repeated forever, on a timetable promised to the millionth of a second. The same sealed box, the same commanded word, the same whisper home. Only the payload differs. And the clock aboard is the most tended clock there is: an atom swinging billions of times a second, disciplined from the ground, its corrections stitched into the very stream, for the blue dot is arithmetic on this stream, and so are the telephone networks below, taking their beat from the sky’s.

door.q: What a clock is, that its ticks can be counted on
Here-and-now, poured like any message

trail.bottom: Control, sense, stream: the machine is the same one that plays your games, in the hardest room there is, and half of it lives on the ground. The primers below are what it is made of; the cards above are what it is for.

door.q: A real machine — the dance, step by step, unattended
The Bit — the spelling of every whisper

trail.title: How software is written
trail.intro: No machine has ever read a word, yet every program begins as words, written by a person. This is the trail between the two: how the written list is shaped, checked, and translated into the numbers a machine will obey.

step.name: the words
step.line: a language small enough to check
step.blurb: English is too loose for a machine: “put the thing near the other thing” could mean anything. So programs are written in languages built the other way round — a few dozen exact words, sentences of a shape agreed in advance, no idiom, no irony, no “you know what I mean”. The smallness is not poverty. It is the price of being understood exactly, every time, by something that has no idea what you mean.

door.q: The one-word tradition — a language small enough for a keypad
The other way to make a machine behave — guessed, not written

step.name: the shape
step.line: every sentence checked against the agreed form
step.blurb: Each sentence must match a shape agreed in advance (this word first, that kind of name second), and before the program ever runs, another walk of it matches sentence after sentence against the shape. Anything crooked is refused at the desk, the line and the word named. The refusal feels like scolding. It is the machine’s equivalent of a friend reading your letter back to you before you send it: every mistake caught here is one that never reaches the sky, the warehouse, or the hospital.

door.q: Match or refuse — a yes-or-no question
Checked against the agreed rules — how the rules are walked

step.name: the translation
step.line: a program that writes programs
step.blurb: The checked list is still words, and the machine still reads none of them. So another program, the translator, walks the list and emits the machine’s own numbers: this exact sentence becomes those few, that one becomes these. The translator is itself a program, written once and borrowed by everyone, and there are two traditions for its timing: translate everything in advance and hand over pure numbers, or read and obey one sentence at a time as it arrives. Either way, what reaches the machine is not words.

door.q: A number that means a command — what the numbers mean
The numbers themselves — spelled in two symbols
Matching a sentence against a shape — the matching craft

step.name: the rooms
step.line: borrowed instructions, written once
step.blurb: Nobody writes the whole list. Programs are assembled from rooms of instructions written by other people (take a picture, open a wire, sort this column), borrowed by the sentence and linked in by the translator, reused for decades by strangers who never meet. Rooms borrow rooms: the sort borrows the compare, the compare borrows the subtract. Most of any program was written by someone else, and that is not laziness. It is the whole craft: composition, exactly as in this deck.

door.q: A room that borrows itself — recursion at ground level
Who keeps the rooms, and hands them out
Rooms written by strangers who never meet — what does the shape of the team do to the shape of the code?
Where does a program really live — in the text, or in the team that built it?

step.name: the tower
step.line: each language standing on another
step.blurb: Stack the rooms and the languages and you get the tower: a language for pages standing on a language for pictures, standing on a language for machines, standing on the one alphabet. The person writes at the top, the machine obeys at the bottom, and the translator is the staircase between floors. No floor understands the one above it — each floor trusts the one below, blindly, exactly. Every app you have ever tapped stood on this tower, and no one who built the top has ever needed to see the bottom.

door.q: The tower primer — how to build well inside it
Where all the floors live while the program runs
Two whole languages built from words this small
How those two languages were found — the trail of the two rivers

trail.bottom: Words, shapes, translation, borrowed rooms, a tower with a machine in the basement: this is how anything at all gets written for a machine that reads nothing. The primers below are the basement and the craft; the trails above are what has been built on it.

door.q: The machine in the basement — the dance, step by step
The tower — how to build well inside it

trail.title: How it finds the answer
trail.intro: Some questions are not computed but looked up: the machine is told only what is true, facts and rules that build new truths from old, and finds the answer by walking. This is the trail of that trick, from the pond of facts to every road at once.

step.name: only the facts
step.line: told what is true, never how to look
step.blurb: Tell the machine no instructions at all. State the facts: this road meets that road, this evening was watched by this household, this order carries these meals. The machine is never told how to find anything, only what is, and every answer it will ever give is already lying in the facts, waiting to be walked. This is programming turned inside out: not a recipe for every question, but a world of truths and questions thrown at it.

door.q: Where the facts park — tables, and the shortcuts that find them
The other way: instructions, written by hand — and what changes when you don’t
A world of truths and rules, walked to its answers — could an organization be one?

step.name: the fit
step.line: a question with holes, tried against every truth
step.blurb: A question is a pattern with holes in it: who begets whom, which road leads where. The machine takes the pattern to the pond and tries it against the facts, one at a time, and each trial is one small yes-or-no: this fact and these holes can be made to agree, or they cannot. Nothing is approximated and nothing is guessed; agreement is a kind of arithmetic, two shapes made equal or rejected, and the machine does it the way it does everything: exactly.

door.q: Every trial a yes-or-no — the fork underneath
The same question, asked everywhere at once

step.name: the walk
step.line: dead ends backed up, untaken roads remembered
step.blurb: A rule’s answer needs other rules’ answers first, so the walk forks: take the first road, and if it dead-ends, back up to the last untaken fork and try the next. That is all backtracking is, the newest untaken road remembered. And the walk contains a copy of itself, answering a rule means walking rules, which is why a search this simple can answer questions nobody wrote a procedure for. The person asks. The machine wanders, exactly, until the wandering is an answer.

door.q: The walk contains a copy of itself — the primer
A recipe that contains itself — the walk, as steps of steps
How the self-containing walk was made honest — the rule that names itself

step.name: all the roads at once
step.line: every branch given its own small machine
step.blurb: The tree of maybes can be walked one road at a time, or it can be staffed: every branch handed to its own small machine, all walking at once, the first answer home declared the winner. The cost is honest and paid in advance: many branches would have been backed out of anyway, so their machines’ work is thrown away. But throwing work away is what machines are for, and the answer that took the short road arrives while the lone walker is still backing up. Speed, here, is a rummaging made wide instead of deep.

door.q: A thousand hands in one pond — who touches what, and who wins
The warehouse that staffs the branches

step.name: which answers
step.line: the first answer, or all of them, said out loud
step.blurb: Some questions have one answer, some have thousands, and the machine does not know which until asked — so the asking says it: the first answer home, or all of them gathered, every answer once. And once the roads run in parallel, the order of the answers is no longer promised: whichever branch wins, wins, and a program that meant one answer must say so out loud, or learn to love whichever arrives. The discipline is small and it is everything: know which question you asked.

door.q: The other way of answering: guesses scored, not facts walked
The query — a language small enough for one line

trail.bottom: Facts, a fit, a walk, every road at once, and the answers said plainly: this is how the machine finds what it was never told. Underneath, it is agreement, shapes that fit, and a walk that contains itself.

door.q: The pond itself — the primer of facts and rules
Recursion — the walk that contains the walk

trail.title: How a world is simulated
trail.intro: To compute a world, tomorrow’s sky, tonight’s flight, the city’s traffic, the machine does one thing: holds the world as numbers, applies a small rule everywhere at once, and repeats on a beat. This is the trail of that pattern, from the state to the rule to the walk.

step.name: the state
step.line: the whole world, held as a block of numbers
step.blurb: First the world must be reduced: the sky to a lattice of cells, the city to corners and edges, the game to positions and scores — everything that matters, rounded into numbers and parked side by side in memory. This is the world as far as the machine will ever know it; there is no other copy, and no oracle to consult. Change the numbers and the world changes. That is all the machine holds of a world, and it is enough.

door.q: How a block of numbers is held against the off switch
The frame buffer — a world of numbers, painted

step.name: the rule
step.line: what happens next, written small
step.blurb: What happens next is not consulted; it is written, by a person, in advance, small: each cell asks only its neighbours, the same question everywhere, and the answer decides what the cell becomes. No cell glances out of the model, and no special case hides in a corner. Smallness is what makes the rule checkable (a person can read it, argue with it, improve it), and it is what makes the future computable at all.

door.q: The rule, unwound — yes-or-no forks
Facts and rules — what a rule is made of

step.name: the beat
step.line: nothing moves until the beat says next
step.blurb: The rule cannot update the world in place, or each cell would half-see the future of its neighbours. So the machine keeps two worlds, the old one it reads and the new one it writes, and on each beat swaps them wholesale: tick becomes tock, tock becomes tick. The whole trick of the beat is that no world is ever written into while it is being read from, an old lesson this deck teaches twice because it bites twice.

door.q: Two worlds, one beat — the honest order
Who gives the beat

step.name: the walk
step.line: from a start, forward, one beat at a time
step.blurb: Once the state, the rule and the beat agree, the future is a walk: apply, swap, apply, swap — each step computed entirely from the last, on and on until tomorrow exists. The launch is flown on the ground the day before it is lit, the forecast is the same walk with weather as its world, and the game you play is the same walk, sixty times a second, waiting for your thumb. Nothing in the walk knows which world it is walking. That is why one pattern serves them all.

door.q: A task that contains a copy of itself — steps of steps
The arithmetic of the walk, and what obeys it

step.name: the many tries
step.line: uncertain beginnings, many worlds
step.blurb: When the beginning is honest about being uncertain (a breeze missed here, a degree missed there), one walk is not the truth. So the machine walks many: forty skies from forty slightly different mornings, a hundred flights from a hundred weathers, and the answers agree at first, then slowly fan out. Confidence, in a computed world, is a count: of all the walks tried, how many brought the rain. It is not a mood, and it is not a guess. It is arithmetic, patiently repeated.

door.q: When the guesses are scored and kept — the learning promise
Many walks at once — the trail of many machines as one

trail.bottom: A world as numbers, a rule small enough to read, a beat to keep the copies honest, and a walk that never asks which world it is walking: this is how the machine holds tomorrow. Underneath, it is the one machine, walking arithmetic, holding numbers.

door.q: Where the world waits between beats
The spelling of every number in the world

trail.title: How many machines act as one
trail.crumb: how many machines act as one
trail.intro: One machine walks one instruction at a time, yet tomorrow’s weather is computed in an afternoon and a warehouse answers ten thousand strangers at once. This is the trail of that trick: the job cut to pieces, the pieces handed out, and the pieces made to wait for each other.

step.name: the split
step.line: one job, cut into pieces that do not touch
step.blurb: The job must first be cut: the sky into regions, the evening’s orders one by one, the film into blocks of frames — pieces as separate as possible, because pieces that touch must talk. The cutting is the whole art: cut well and the machines barely speak; cut badly and they spend the afternoon waiting for each other’s numbers. A good cut looks obvious afterwards, the way all good arrangements do.

door.q: Chopped, numbered, handed on — the trail of pieces
Who does the cutting — the manager’s oldest move

step.name: the handout
step.line: the manager walks the room with the pieces
step.blurb: A manager, a program on a machine like every manager in this deck, walks the room with the basket: an idle box gets a piece, a fast box gets two, a struggling box is passed over without ceremony. No box is asked its opinion, and no box knows the shape of the whole job. Ten thousand strangers’ orders leave a warehouse this way, every evening, and none of the boxes doing it understands dinner.

door.q: The scheduler, at warehouse scale
Two hands, one basket — the honest order

step.name: the shared edges
step.line: the pieces trade their borders, every beat
step.blurb: The pieces are never perfectly apart: my region of sky borders yours, and my next minute depends on your edge cells. So on every beat the machines trade their borders — one row of numbers across the wire, chopped, enveloped, kept until received like any message. The machines are neighbours in two senses: side by side in the room, and side by side in the world they are computing.

door.q: The borders cross the wire — the trail of a message
Where the traded border parks between beats

step.name: the barrier
step.line: no box may run ahead of the slowest
step.blurb: At the end of each beat there is a gate: no box begins the next piece until every box has finished the last, because a fast box racing ahead would compute a future from a missing past. The whole room waits for its slowest member — maddening, and unavoidable: acting as one means being no faster than the slowest agreement. Every world walked on many machines pays this toll, every beat, all afternoon.

door.q: The wait is the agreement — one cell, two writers, one order
Step or wait: a fork at every beat

step.name: the one machine, wearing a warehouse
step.line: to the program, a strange-shaped machine
step.blurb: To the person writing the program, the warehouse is one machine with a strange shape: a thousand processors, a wire inside, a manager in the middle. To the weather it is tomorrow arriving on time. To each box it is nothing at all — alone in the room, running its dance, holding its numbers, waiting at the gate. Nothing exotic was added to make many act as one. The one design was multiplied, and then taught to wait for itself.

door.q: The one design, in every box
The dance each box runs, step by step

trail.bottom: Cut, handed out, traded at the borders, held at the gate: many machines act as one by pretending to be one machine, slowly and by agreement. Each box is the machine the other trails explain; the wire between them is a trail of its own.

door.q: The wire between the boxes — the trail of a message
A real machine — the box every piece runs on

trail.title: When two hands meet
trail.intro: Parallel means many things done at once, for speed; concurrent means many things that must meet, whatever the clock does with them. This is the trail of the meeting: one cell, two writers, and every arrangement a machine can make so the two never spoil each other’s work.

step.name: the meeting
step.line: two writers, one cell, no promised order
step.blurb: Two workers share one cell, and each runs the same three lines: read it, add one, write it back. Alone, each is honest; together, in the unlucky order where both read before either writes, two increments become one, the sum silently loses, and the test that passed yesterday fails at three in the morning, under load, when no one is watching. The bug is not in either worker. It is in the gap between a read and a write, which the cell promised no one would ever stand in.

door.q: The cell itself — how a number is held against everyone
One instruction at a time, order for free — the world this trail leaves

step.name: the doorman
step.line: one in the room, the others at the door
step.blurb: The oldest cure is a door with one key: a worker takes the key, does all three lines, returns the key, and only then does the next worker enter. It works, it has carried fifty years of correct systems, but it is a discipline kept by hand: the key must be asked for in a settled order, held briefly, returned on every path, even the paths that fail. One forgotten return and the room locks forever; one impatient order and two keys wait on each other, a circle no one can leave. The doorman is a promise, and promises are kept by the tired.

door.q: The manager as doorman — who runs the door
The warehouse: many machines, one agreed room

step.name: the mail
step.line: don’t share the cell: post to its owner
step.blurb: The other road takes the sharing away. The workers never touch the cell: each drops a small note, add one, into a pipe, and the pipe has an owner whose whole job is taking the notes one at a time, in whatever order they arrive, and doing the work alone. Nothing is lost, nothing locks, and no arrival order changes the answer, because one hand holds the cell at every instant, and two stories cannot disagree where there is never a second story. The pipe is not a faster lock. It is the end of sharing, and the notes are messages, exactly like the wire’s — only shorter.

door.q: A message, chopped, kept until received — now inside one machine
The primer of the cell: one latch, one hand

step.name: the single hand
step.line: written once, read forever, or not yet
step.blurb: The deepest cure is written into the language itself: a cell that may be written once, by one writer, and never overwritten. Any eye that looks before the writing does not get a wrong answer — it waits. The wait is the agreement: the reader hangs mid-thought until the writer settles the value, then resumes as if nothing had happened. No locks, no keys, no doormen; the meeting’s order no longer matters because nothing is ever revised, only completed. A whole family of languages is built on this one arrangement, and their programs have no races for the same reason the sand has no weather: the storms were made unsayable.

door.q: Never write while reading — the two worlds, swapped wholesale
The primer of agreement — facts that fit or wait

step.name: the honest orders
step.line: any meeting allowed, one answer required
step.blurb: Once hands can meet in any order, honesty gets a stricter meaning: the program must land the same answer whatever the scheduler does, and the programmer confesses, up front, that the order is not promised. A machine sealed in the sky cannot be debugged at three in the morning; a car’s hundred little machines cannot be stepped through one meeting at a time. So correctness is designed for every interleaving at once, tested on one, then two, then eight, and where any winner will do, the program says so out loud, and takes the first answer home.

door.q: All roads at once, any winner honest — the search run in parallel
The sealed machine: no one comes to debug, so every order must already agree

trail.bottom: A meeting, a doorman, a mailbox, a single hand, an honest answer: this is how many acts share one world without spoiling it. Underneath, it is time, the order things happen in, and the memory they happen to.

door.q: Time — the primer of order itself
Memory — the cell, the latch, and the warning in it

trail.title: How everything fails
trail.intro: Nothing built works perfectly, and the bigger the thing, the truer that is. This is the trail of failure itself: the infinite ways a system can break, the safeguards that break by protecting, and the one law that separates the systems that work from the systems that are merely designed.

step.name: the law of failure
step.line: a system can fail in an infinite number of ways
step.blurb: A system can fail in an infinite number of ways. That is the fundamental theorem, and its corollary is crueler: the mode of failure cannot be read from the structure. The diagram says what the system does when it works; the failure arrives from outside the diagram — a storm, a typo, a late supplier, a tired operator at three in the morning. Two systems built alike fail unalike, and the deciding variable is discovered by accident, years in, at the worst moment. So the honest designer starts from the law: whatever is built will break, and not where the drawing says it will.

door.q: the bug that needs two workers and one unlucky order — a failure born between the parts, invisible to them
the drift that breaks a working system from the inside
the first theorem of the new machines — no rule can say which programs finish

step.name: the hidden rot
step.line: broken, and working anyway
step.blurb: The second theorem is worse: any large system is operating most of the time in failure mode, degraded, partial, limping, and the malfunction may not be detectable for long periods, if ever. The user does not see it because the system does not stop, and the operator does not see it because the dials watch what the system was designed to do, not what it has quietly stopped doing. And a large system is beyond anyone’s capacity to evaluate: no one holds the whole machine in mind, so no one can certify it whole. Failure is not an exception that arrives one day; it is the weather the system already lives in.

door.q: the manager — the one room meant to see the whole machine
the promise of dials that watch what the system has stopped doing

step.name: the safeguard that fails
step.line: the protection becomes the hazard
step.blurb: The most dangerous part of a system is the part added to make it safe. When a fail-safe fails, it fails by failing to fail safe: the load-shedding device sheds so eagerly that the rest of the grid is oversupplied and the great generators shut down, the anti-meltdown device causes the very melt it was built for, and the reactor’s automatic shutdown cannot even say where the trouble is. Every protection is more system, and more system is more ways to fail — the cure is a patient too. So a safeguard earns double respect: it must work, and its own failure must itself be survivable.

door.q: the barrier — an agreement that, when it fails, fails by stopping everything at once
the one design every safeguard borrows — and the thing that must also fail

step.name: the simple that works
step.line: grown from a working simple thing
step.blurb: Yet some complex systems work, and the law of their success is older than computers: a complex system that works is invariably found to have evolved from a simple system that worked. The one designed from scratch, whole and perfect, never works and cannot be patched — it must be started over, beginning with a working simple thing. This is not modesty; it is the only road that arrives, because every working part was already working before it was assembled. The sand obeys the law twice over: the universal machine, the simplest complete system there is, and the tower of languages grown on top of it, one working layer at a time.

door.q: the primer of the tower — language grown on language, none of it designed whole
rooms borrowing rooms — the tower, climbed by a real trail

step.name: the fallback
step.line: when it cannot do everything, it does something
step.blurb: The working answer is a hierarchy of tasks. The top task is the whole service; each task below it is a smaller promise, easier to keep: reduced, but still worth having. When an error cannot be corrected, the system does not limp on half-broken: it abandons the top task and performs the simpler one. The satellite drops to its safe mode, the phone still sends texts when the map app dies, and the airliner keeps flying on what remains. Failure is not the end of the design — it is one of the designed behaviours, met with a smaller promise, kept.

door.q: the sealed machine — the safe mode that must work with no one aboard
the trail of the walls and the watchers — how the fallback is built

trail.bottom: An infinite number of ways to fail, a safeguard that is one of them, a simplicity that survives, and a smaller promise to keep: this is how systems meet their own failure. Underneath, it is the universal machine, the working simple thing, and the tower grown from it.

door.q: the Turing machine — the working simple system everything else evolved from
the tower — the complex, grown one language at a time

trail.title: How the whole survives
trail.intro: Every large program contains errors, however carefully it was tested. The honest question is not how to write a perfect program but how to build a whole that keeps its promise while its parts misbehave: walls between the parts, watchers over the workers, and the strange result — a system of parts that all fail, running for years without ever being down.

step.name: the walls
step.line: one part breaks, only that part breaks
step.blurb: The essential problem of fault tolerance is isolation: different programmers write different modules, some correct and some not, and an error in one must not spoil the others. The cure is the oldest boundary in computing — the process, a small walled room with its own memory and no shared keys, where nothing passes the wall except copies, handed across like notes. One room may burn while the others keep working, because they never shared a floor. And the wall must live in the language itself, built before the first bug, not raised after the first fire.

door.q: share nothing — the mail road, taken to its end
the manager — the rooms, assigned and cleaned up

step.name: the crash as message
step.line: the failure travels, and is answered elsewhere
step.blurb: When a room burns, the others hear of it, because the burn itself is turned into a message: a note saying who died and why, delivered to whoever was set to care. A machine’s death is dressed in the same envelope as a crashed program’s, one uniform way to learn of loss, near or far, so the system never needs two kinds of sorry. And the error is handled not where it happened but somewhere else, by someone else: a strange idea inside one program, and the only idea that survives distribution. Failure, underneath, has become data.

door.q: a message, chopped, kept until received — even the news of a death
the answer found by walking facts — and a crash is one of the facts

step.name: let it crash
step.line: if you cannot do what you wanted, die
step.blurb: The slogans sound like surrender and are the opposite: let some other process fix the error, die when you cannot do what you wanted, never program defensively. The worker’s code stays clean (no nets, no guessing at recovery, no branch written blind for a failure its author cannot reproduce), because the worker is allowed to fail and someone else is paid to care. Defensive code is the bug’s best hiding place: it swallows the error and limps, corrupting quietly for weeks. The honest program tries, and when it cannot, it stops, loudly and leaving a note, and the recovery lives in another room, written by another hand.

door.q: never written while reading — the world a crash cannot corrupt
the alarm that knows what rang it — the crash, made visible

step.name: the watcher
step.line: one does the work, another watches it fail
step.blurb: So the system is built from two kinds of rooms: workers, which do the job, and supervisors, which watch workers. A supervisor answers no requests and holds no pencils; it waits for the notes that say a worker died, and answers each with a policy — start it again, wait a moment and start it again, start it five times and then give up and report upward. The watchers are watched in turn, a tree of them, small above big, so no failure is ever orphaned, all the way to the root, where the last watcher replaces a whole branch and the phone call is never made. The code that fails and the code that recovers live in different bodies, and neither clutters the other.

door.q: the manager — keeping the machine busy, and starting it again
the primer of the tree — a watcher of watchers is recursion

step.name: the unreliable parts
step.line: every part fails; the whole does not
step.blurb: The last wall is geography: a whole computer will die, so the work must live in two. Pairs of processes watch each other the way pairs of computers do, each prepared to take the other’s calls; the warehouse answers from several identical machines so that no machine is ever the only one. The parts are not made reliable. That is the discovery: the parts are assumed unreliable and arranged so their failures cancel. A telephone switch with a million lines of code is run this way, and its downtime is seconds a year: not because nothing failed, but because everything that failed was expected, noticed, and answered by its twin.

door.q: the barrier and the handout — the warehouse this trail relies on
no one in charge — the copies that must agree without a boss

trail.bottom: Walls, a crash that travels, a watcher for every worker, and a twin for every whole: this is how a system keeps its promise while its parts break. Underneath, it is the machine that starts again, one instruction at a time, and the tree the watchers grow.

door.q: a real machine — the fetch, the decode, and the restart
recursion — the watcher of watchers, all the way down

trail.title: How the copies stay one
trail.intro: Almost every service worth using is now many machines wearing one name. This is the trail of that arrangement: the copies that make failure ordinary, the asks that are safe to repeat, the shards that cut the world into owned pieces, and the election that decides, among equals, who decides.

step.name: the study of failure
step.line: the design begins with the way things fail
step.blurb: Designing a distributed system is, in one author’s phrase, the study of how systems fail: the design begins at the failure and works backwards. The failure arrives from everywhere at once: the request crosses a wire that loses things, lands on a machine that restarts, is answered by a program replaced mid-flight. The answer is not to make each part perfect; it is to arrange ordinary failing parts so the service does not inherit their failures: enough copies that one is always alive, asks that are safe to repeat, and an owner that can be replaced while the work goes on. Nothing in the design is exotic — every piece is a small plain idea, arranged.

door.q: the general law — every system fails in more ways than it has parts
the warehouse (split, handout, barrier), the shape being kept alive

step.name: the copies
step.line: one name, many machines behind it
step.blurb: The first arrangement is the oldest: several identical workers behind one front door. The door spreads the work across them, and none is indispensable: a machine may die mid-shift and the door never mentions it, and new copies are wheeled in while the queue drains. What makes it work is that a copy holds nothing the others lack: any copy can answer any request, because the memory of the conversation lives in a shared store, not inside the worker. A worker that remembers nothing private can be replaced in a heartbeat — and a worker that can be replaced can be allowed to fail.

door.q: the promise of the shared memory all the copies borrow
one name that must find one live machine — the wire’s oldest promise

step.name: the safe repeat
step.line: asked once or asked again, the same answer
step.blurb: A wire that loses things must be allowed to try again, and a retry is only safe if the ask is idempotent: performed once or performed five times, the same answer. Setting a value is safe, the register is five however many times it is said, and counting is not: add one, and a retry buys a second one. So the ask is redesigned until it is safe to repeat: the delivery is at-least-once, and the receiver makes the extra arrivals harmless, remembering which asks it has already answered. The whole system rests on a small stubborn habit, when in doubt ask again, and the habit is made honest by design, not by luck.

door.q: two increments become one — the bug that makes counting unsafe to repeat
the same walk, the same answer — a question that may be asked again for free

step.name: the shards
step.line: cut the world into pieces, each piece owned
step.blurb: When no set of copies can hold the whole world, the world is cut instead: each machine owns one slice of the data, a range of names, a region of the map, a band of accounts, and every ask is routed first to its owner, then answered from memory the owner really has. And when no single slice can answer (a search across everything, a question about all the cells at once), the ask is fanned out to all the shards at once and the answers race home: the first good one is accepted, the stragglers discarded. The cut is chosen with care, for a bad cut makes pieces that talk too much; the fan-out is a search run wide, and any honest winner will do.

door.q: the grid — the sky cut into a lattice of numbered cells, a cut chosen with the same care
the promise of the route — how an ask finds its owner among the pieces

step.name: the elected leader
step.line: whoever is alive and noticed, leads
step.blurb: Some work must be done by exactly one machine at a time: the copy that writes the file, the node that hands out addresses, the process that sets the order. Appointing one is fatal, the appointed dies and takes the office with it, so the system elects instead, and the election has no ballots and no authority: the lease. A leader is simply the copy whose ticket has not yet expired, and the others follow it because they can all see the clock; when it dies, the ticket lapses, and whoever is alive and noticed takes the office. Establishing ownership this way is the hardest part of a reliable distributed system: deciding who decides, without anyone in charge of the deciding.

door.q: one ledger, no double spend — election made unforgeable
the primer of order — the lease is a timeout with an office attached

trail.bottom: Copies that may fail, asks that may be repeated, shards that may be owned, a leader that may be replaced: this is how one name is worn by many machines. Underneath, it is the memory the copies must agree on — and the time by which they take turns.

door.q: memory — the state the copies keep identical, or agree to split
time — which copy wrote first, and whose lease has lapsed

trail.title: How a camera sees
trail.intro: The image trail ends where the numbers are shown, lamp by lamp; this is the trail of where the numbers come from. Light is caught in a lattice of tiny wells, emptied and measured one row at a time, until the world in front of the lens has become a grid of numbers. The ear has its drum and the eye has its wells: this is the eye’s half of the story, the picture’s missing half.

step.name: the well
step.line: a tiny bucket that light fills
step.blurb: A camera’s smallest part is a bucket for light. A well of silicon, struck by a photon, loses an electron to the strike; the electron is held in the well, and the well keeps every one it catches. Brighter light, more strikes, a fuller bucket: the well does not see, it collects, and it holds what it collects as charge, silently, until someone comes to empty it and ask how much. This is the same two-step as the ear’s drum (the world arrives, is caught, and waits to be measured), with light standing in for pressure and silicon standing in for air.

door.q: the trick in general — anything caught, held, and read into a number
pressure, then number — the ear’s two steps, the eye’s two steps

step.name: the lattice
step.line: millions of wells, one per point
step.blurb: One well catches one point; a picture needs all of them at once. So the wells are laid out in a strict grid, millions deep, and a lens is set in front to bend the world onto it: every point of the scene falls on its own well, the whole view divided before a single number exists. The two-million-pixel grid of the image trail is this lattice seen from the other side (there it wears lamps, here it wears wells), and the satellite’s whole sky is read the same way, well by well, a picture of the Earth arriving as a page of charges.

door.q: the same grid, wearing lamps — the half that shows
the senses of the sealed machine — a whole sky, read well by well

step.name: the readout
step.line: emptied and measured, row by row
step.blurb: Then the buckets are emptied, in strict order: a row is tipped out, each charge counted and rounded to a number, then the next row. The counting is the measure trail’s ladder in silicon, the charge compared against rungs of known value, landed on the nearest, written down, and the whole grid, millions of wells, is read in a few hundredths of a second, one well at a time, while the next frame gathers. A grid of charges becomes a page of numbers, parked, ready to be shown, stored, or poured down to the ground.

door.q: millions of wells read one at a time — the switching illusion
where the frame parks until it is needed

step.name: the colours
step.line: one filter per well, three numbers per point
step.blurb: A well is blind to colour: it counts light, not its shade. So a mosaic of tiny filters is laid over the lattice — red, green, blue, one per well, in a pattern that favours green, because the eye itself favours it. Each well then reports not light but its colour of light, and the missing two of the three at every point are guessed from next door, the neighbours’ numbers averaged in. The eye is flattered twice: once by the green-heavy pattern, once by the honest guess. And the three numbers per point that the image trail lights lamp by lamp are born here, guessed in part, and true enough.

door.q: the missing values guessed from their neighbours — the promise of guesses scored and kept
the pipeline that turns these numbers back into a picture — the trail of the painting

step.name: the honest eye
step.line: it does not see; it measures
step.blurb: The confession: a camera does not see. It measures — and every measure rounds, every well leaks a little, every grid has wells that lie (a stuck pixel, a hot pixel, a mote of dust), and heat adds its own false light to every frame. So the craft is honest about its instrument: dark frames are taken with the lens closed to learn the heat’s own signature, flat fields are taken of nothing to learn each well’s private bias, and the camera’s numbers are corrected against the camera before anyone believes them. The most watched sensor in the deck is the satellite’s, whose every frame arrives with its own confession attached.

door.q: the sensor as a system: it drifts, it lies a little — failure designed for, frame by frame
the dark frame, the calibration numbers — the sensor reporting on itself

trail.bottom: A well for light, a lattice of them, a readout one row at a time, a guess for the colours, and a confession: this is how the world becomes the numbers a picture is. Underneath, it is the number each well is emptied into — and the frame of numbers, held.

door.q: the Bit — the spelling of every number the wells give up
memory — the frame, held while the next is caught

trail.title: How a clock keeps time
trail.intro: Nothing in a machine knows what a second is. The machine is told, by a thing that swings: a crystal squeezed, ringing like a bell, its swings counted one by one. This is the trail of the telling — the swing, the count, the correction every swing needs, the many beats of one machine, and the treaty that lets the whole world agree on now.

step.name: the swing
step.line: a thing that repeats without tiring
step.blurb: Time enters a machine the way sound enters the ear: as a thing that repeats. A pendulum repeats, a balance wheel repeats, and in every machine made, the repeating thing is a sliver of quartz. Squeezed, it answers with a spark, the piezoelectric effect, a charge that comes and goes with the squeeze, and struck once, it rings like a bell at a pace fixed by its cut: a few million times a second in a computer, 32,768 times in a watch. The swing is chosen because it does not tire and barely drifts: the most regular thing a few cents can buy.

door.q: who says when to freeze — the beat every freeze waits on
